content.content:
A listed id that names a node document is underlined while the pointer rests over it. In the detail panel's four relationship sections (rmovtvkt) an entry that names a node is presented as a link (mwwxxzyk); this decision gives that link one further appearance state. While the pointer is over the entry, the id's characters carry an underline. The underline follows the pointer's presence and nothing else: arriving over the entry puts it there, leaving takes it away, and the entry is drawn as it was before the pointer came. The entry is the same link before the pointer arrives and after it leaves — hovering does not create the link, does not make an entry followable that was not, and does not change what the entry is; it adds a mark to an entry that already carries the link look.

The underline is the whole of what changes. The entry's text stays the bare id, as mwwxxzyk fixed it: the underline marks the characters the entry already shows, and while hovered the id is neither shortened, relabelled nor replaced, and no label, summary, quoted title or icon appears beside it, over it or in its place. Nor does the mark reach beyond the entry's own text: it does not run across the rest of the section, and the entry gains no box, badge or border from it. What distinguishes the hovered entry from its neighbours is that mark on the id and nothing else this decision adds.

Underlined is exactly the population mwwxxzyk made a link: an id listed inside one of the four relationship sections that names a node document, whether that document is a decision or an evaluation (zkvxornu). An id the panel mentions anywhere else — in the selected node's kind, content or rationale text, on the canvas, or in a section's empty state — gains nothing here, as it gained nothing from mwwxxzyk. And the state belongs to the entry under the pointer: hovering one listed id underlines that entry, while the other entries in its section and the sections beside it keep their resting appearance.

This is the hover state and no more than it. The colour role the entry takes is tvoouwkn's; the pointer cursor over it is rqrlnzny's; the marker it carries while it has keyboard focus is vvzptxmz's, which is a different state at a different time, and this decision says nothing about how an entry is drawn when it is focused but not hovered. Whether the entry's colour, weight or spacing changes while hovered, and whether anything in the section shifts in size or layout when the pointer enters, are not decided here: nothing in this decision requires or forbids any such change, and none of them may be read off the underline. Nothing here names or invents a class, a selector, a style property or a stylesheet rule, nor the vocabulary that carries the underline; sqwusxql settles the class names and the styling decisions that own them settle how the line is drawn.

An id that names no node document is outside this decision. rusopkql kept such an id listed in its section and inert when activated, and mplxzxnm and kpkstnps settle how it is presented and that it takes no pointer, hover or focus cue. This decision commits the underline for an entry that names a node, and neither requires nor forbids any hover appearance for an entry that names none.
content.rationale:
A link that already looks like a link at rest has one cheap thing left to say: when the pointer is over it, the link answers. The underline is the smallest answer available — it borrows a convention readers apply to text they can follow, it needs no new element, no new text and no change to the id, and it can appear and disappear with the pointer while everything else about the entry stays put. Without it the entry's promise is made once at rest and then the section goes quiet under the pointer, so a reader moving across a list gets no sign of which entry the pointer is on; the underline hands the pointer's position back to the reader as a fact about the entry rather than leaving it to be guessed from the cursor alone.

Stopping at 'underlined while hovered' is what keeps the rest decidable. Everything the underline could be confused with is a separate fact with its own check: the entry's resting colour is a colour role, the cursor is the pointer's own affair, the focus marker is the keyboard's counterpart to this state and has to stay distinguishable from it, and the entry that names no node is a different case on purpose. Settled here, any of them would either restate the decision that owns it or narrow it, and the difference between a hover state and the link it decorates would blur. Kept to one state, this decision leaves each of those to be argued and checked on its own evidence.

What this decision must not do is touch mwwxxzyk's commitment, and it does not: it adds a state to an entry that is already a link, changes neither the text nor the population of entries and adds no element to the panel, so the licence the edge gave is used as narrowly as it was given — a hover state of the link, not a re-decision of what the link is or of which ids are links.
